One commentator has described modern metropolitan areas in the following manner:
In broad terms, the largest metropolitan areas have been evolving rather rapidly into two easily identifiable, although heavily overlapping, subeconomies. The central city is more and more a place of business, professional, and governmental service - the workplace of lawyers, consultants, financiers, and officials of all kinds; the suburbs are more and more the heart of the manufacturing district. Retail trade and personal services are performed in both places, convenient to their customers. One of the main forces which integrate these "dual economies" is long distance commuting to work; suburban white-collar workers heading downtown in the morning pass blue-collar workers from the central city heading for outlying plants and domestics on the way to suburban residences. Thompson, Preface to Suburban Economics, in THE URBANIZATION OF THE SUBURBS, 411 (L. Masotti and J. Hadden eds. 1973).
